en: The musketeers could not fire.
While they stood in confusion,
Allah's sun grew overcast in the sky.
Upon your father's head
Sixty tribulations came at once.
His heart was sorely shaken,
His death seemed close.
Your father spoke his sorrow
At this world's falsehood.
Your lion father remembered
Those who shared his road unto Judgment,
As the unbelievers pressed him hard—
His champions, the forty choros.
Your hero, famed as ‘Manas the hero,’
His dear eyes like a saker falcon's,
Was filled with grievous sorrow;
Unblinking, he gathered tears in his eyes.
Lamenting in distress,
Despairing of his precious life,
He groaned, missing his forty choros.
When the mass of champions and Kozkaman
Surrounded your father Khan Manas,
Despairing of his precious life,
My bloodthirsty lord was left longing for his forty choros.
“The malicious Kalmyks—
O God, I have come here to see them!
My doom written thus,
O God, I have come here to die.
Before death arrives and my soul departs,
The humiliations of living
I have come to suffer from the Kalmyks.
Calling the Chinese my kin,
Utterly deceived, my poor head
I have come here to lose.
Precious food that would burst the gall,
From the hands of these Chinese,
I have come here to consume.
Into the Chinese dungeon forty rope-lengths deep,
I have come here to fall.
This poison measured out for forty years,
I have come here to drink.
Wandering in force from Beezhin,
You all settled in Talas.
Did you eat my foal suckled by two mares,
You cur of wretched stock?
Did you say you would be my equal and my kinsman?
You steeped poison in your barrel;
Worthless cur, thus you brought me to my end.
My banner on the dark spear,
Alas, Almam, my lion!
My gift come from the Kalmyks!
With your waist firmly girded,
Though seven hosts of enemies came,
You would enter and attack with your coat flung open.
My partner in possessions in this world,
Alas, Almam, my brother in faith,
Where have you gone, nowhere to be seen?
Alas, Almam, my companion of the same age!
When I dwelt in Talas,
I used to eat slices of horse rump.
‘If Almambet is beside me,
I shall overthrow the generals,’ I used to say.”
(His wits fled, his heart burned;
My king lamented,
Longing there for his forty choros.)
Wearing a gray lynx-fur cap,
Wielding a mottled blue shield,
His head adorned all over with gold,
His feet supported by a thousand gold pieces,
Finding words in a sudden crisis,
Finding sight in the dark night,
Rinsing his mouth with honey,
The suffering of six months
He discerned in the blink of an eye.
Sent ahead, he brought good fortune;
Following me, he was like countless troops.
The falcon of humankind,
The foal of saintly wisdom,
My towering figure before me,
King Bakai, my support—
Almambet and Bakai, peerless lions,
If only these two stood watching!
Then let the rotten men come from the Kalmyks,
Whose hems never touch the ground,
Who do not sit to urinate,
The uncircumcised who know no faith,
Try to do this then!
Going before the caliph, he received a writ;
From a saint he received a blessing;
He pledged himself to twelve spiritual masters.
He was called a mighty conqueror,
Wore a blue coat of ribbed cloth,
Rode a splendid mottled blue horse.
None could overcome him in a struggle;
A lion's teeth could not pierce him.
With piercing shouts and ringing battle cries,
Akbaltai's lion—
I, Manas, have sinned against Allah!
Where has he gone, leaving no trace,
That lion of mine, Chubak?
When I dwelt in Talas,
I used to eat slices of horse-belly fat.
‘If Chubak the leopard is with me,
I shall overthrow the Kalmyks,’ I used to say.
My leopard Chubak, my wolf-like hero,
If only he stood watching beside me,
Then let the black-thorn Kalmyks
Try to inflict this humiliation!
When the stars stirred in the heavens,
He became my friend for the other world.
We joined together when tiny as lice,
United when small as thumbs.
Honing his sharp tongue,
Knowing seventy different languages,
Speaking eloquently before the khan—
My sworn friend Azhybai,
If only my peerless one stood watching,
Then let the scoundrels come from the Kalmyks
Try to inflict this humiliation!
Light on a horse, a fit rider for a yearling,
Sleeping little, alert upon the road,
Never resting upon his elbow,
Never taking even a brief nap,
Keeping his sword against its sheath,
If many eager foes came forth,
He drenched them in crimson blood.
Riding a strong, enduring steed,
Wearing a deep-blue coat hard as iron,
My swift steed for riding to Altai,
Where has he gone, leaving no trace?
Alas, my kinsman Syrgak!
Syrgak, my nest-mate at my side,
If only the leopard stood watching,
Then let the swine of the dark faith
Try to impose their violence!
My agile Serek—
When the foe came rushing,
My champion who entered without flinching,
While his generous lord lies thus,
Not once does he appear before my eyes.
Where has my champion gone?
If only my Serek stood watching,
Then let the Chinese give poison like a dreadful sickness
And try to impose their violence!
This world is a merchant;
If only Manas could die without looking back!
Not one of the forty choros is here.
My damned, desolate head!
If the mighty warriors were beside me,
Then I could die!
On journeys, he was like countless troops.
My days have turned terribly awry.
Kara the diviner, bringer of good fortune,
Cast his divinations and spoke truly;
Of death and suffering
He spoke firmly, without distortion.
Exulting in his valor,
He joined his precious friend.
If only the diviner stood watching,
Then let these unbelievers
Try to inflict this humiliation!
Yraman's singer,
The discerning judge of human cunning,
Sang the words I spoke.
When I suffered humiliation in many lands,
Often he found a way for me.
He joined what had broken in my life,
Never stood idle in battle.
If only my singer stood watching,
Then let the faithless Chinese
Try to inflict humiliation!
My warrior Shuutu, with a hat like roof felt,
The falcon of humankind,
Bringing good fortune when sent into battle,
By his cunning worth countless troops,
That dear man born to bring good fortune,
The falcon of the forty choros,
Who scouted with me,
Who seized horses from foreign speakers with me,
Who shouted and thrust his spear with me,
Who joined me in pursuit—
Our sheep shared one fold,
We were close companions at the feast.
If my peerless hero Shuutu
Only stood watching here,
Then let the swine who fled from Khangai
Try to inflict their violence;
Then let my precious head perish!
My strong-armed Baichoro,
Exulting in his valor,
Whom I met when he was fourteen,
My man who stands beneath the banner,
Granted by the one God in his favor,
My black-blazed hawk,
Whom I long to behold,
When bloody war and turmoil break out,
My man who stands beneath the banner:
When I look, he is nowhere to be seen;
No one knows where he is.
I am suffering this oppression;
It is my hour to die.
Where has my dear companion Baichoro gone?
If only he would charge and thrust his spear,
If only Baichoro, my support, stood watching,
Then let Manas die,
And behold the other world!
I have suffered calamity from the unbelievers;
If I die, it will be disgrace.
If only my Baichoro would come here,
His king Manas—
If only he would look upon him!
Kyrgylchal, leader of the forty,
That mad old man, swaggering among the forty.
In the bitter forty days of winter,
Who turned his old wife upside down forty times,
The lusty old man who could couple forty times a night:
If only he would raise a piercing cry!
When the unbelievers brought calamity,
If only Kyrgylchal would come shouting
And rescue me!
Who thrust his spear untiringly—
If only Tazbaimat stood watching!
I have grown faint, all alone.
Then let these Chinese
Try to inflict this violence!
Ormonbek, son of Khan Odugan,
My warrior choro with a saint's nature,
My devastating choro, my hero, is absent.
What we see today is gone tomorrow;
Were you always like this, filthy world?
Your wisdom none could match.
When I consider carefully,
He would rescue me and raise a tumult—
Alas, Bozuul, my dear companion!
Ormonbek and Bozuul, that pair,
My oceans, if only they stood watching,
Then let the Black Chinese and the Manchu dogs
Try to inflict humiliation!
My fortress with iron ramparts,
My far-seeing, wolf-like Korogoch,
My swift steed for riding to Altai,
Who made the distant near,
Wolf-like Korogoch is not here.
If only Korogoch stood watching,
Then let the unbelievers of the dark faith
Try to impose their violence!
No lord is here, no khan of mine.
Would God strike me into darkness?
All forty mighty warriors are absent.
I have no support to rely upon,
No place in which to shelter.
She who joined me when tiny as a louse,
Who united with me when small as a thumb,
Whom I met when tiny as a tick,
The dusky beauty,
The radiant one among Muslims,
